chapter: The Famous Door, Billy May and the Palomar fire
title: Famous Door personnel, the Paramount Theater and Glenn Miller taking Billy May
summary: He describes Nat Jaffe, Bob Burnett and Johnny Mendel, Billy May stepping in as trumpeter at the Paramount Theater, and Glenn Miller hiring him by mistake.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Who was in the band when you opened at the Famous Door?

Well, actually there were -- well, we had a wonderful piano player by the name of Nat Jaffe, who was -- he was like Tatum, you know. He wasn't the greatest band piano player in the world, but he had a technique like Art's. I mean he was just fantastic. And the rest of the guys in the band were -- there weren't really any stars. Bobby Burnett was in that band, a trumpet player who was with me for quite awhile after that, there, and later. And we really didn't have -- it was more or less of a team effort, rather than a bunch of -- there weren't any stars, so as to speak, outside of possibly Jaffe and Bob Burnett. We did have a very

singular person by the name of Johnny Mendel, not Mandel, but Johnny Mendel, out of Chicago. He was -- that wasn't his real name. He was Polish, and he was one of the sole remaining guys that knew how to growl and use a plunger. And he was in the band. And he played a particularly beautiful solo on a thing that Barney Bigard wrote, called, "Meant For a Lost Love." It's a muted solo with a harmon mute the -- it's one of the prettiest things. I still play it every now and then, when I think of it, because it's so pretty, what Johnny Mendel played on that. But he was kind of a crotchety old man then, I mean, anyway. You know, he was much older than all of us, and -- but nevertheless, the band was enthusiastic. That's the whole thing. And they imparted this to the people, and we had good arrangements, and that was about the size of it. And things went along. We went into the Paramount Theater, my first time in the Paramount Theater, with Dorothy Lamour and Mischa Auer, and that was our first of quite a few Paramount engagements. And that was when we had to press Billy into service as a trumpet player. By that time we had a first trumpet player by the name of Charlie Huffine, and Charlie got a bad lip or got sick, I don't know, or he didn't show up, I don't know. For some reason he wasn't there. And I said, "You play trumpet, " to Billy. I said, "You've got to step in there." Well, as far as I know he hadn't touched the trumpet the whole time he was in New York. I know he didn't touch it because we were living together. And he got the trumpet and he took over the first

trumpet chair and played it unbelievably well. Which of course he wasn't a first trumpet player, but he knew all the charts because he'd written them. And what he couldn't do he'd say, "You play that," you know, and that's when Billy became actually a playing arranger with my band. But in fact that's when we went to four trumpets, because we'd only had three up to that point with that band. And, oh, a couple of years later Glenn Miller stole Billy from me, but he did it by accident. Actually this is very funny. He told his manager, he said, "Find out the guy that's playing that jazz with Charlie Barnett. I want him." Well, actually it was Bob Burnett that was playing all the jazz, and the guy happened to come in when Billy was playing one of his three jazz solos, and Glenn hired Billy instead of Bob, which actually, although I love Bob dearly, and he was you know, pretty much a part of everything, to lose Billy then was quite a loss, because Billy had been the backbone of the arranging. He had written "Cherokee," and "Pompton Turnpike," and a lot of the other records of that time. That They were most important to us, and I hated to lose him. But I lost him on a fluke.
Glenn Miller could pay a lot more?
Oh, sure. Glenn was already very big.
